source.title: MPSelectTune: Prompt-type Selection for Fine-tuning improves Concept Unlearning in LLMs
source.authors: Shubhadip Nag; Srinjoy Das; Agniva Saha; Anushree Ghosh; Soumi Das; Tarun Kumar; Suparna Bhattacharya; Sourangshu Bhattacharya

page_placements.theme: Prompt variants leave more residual than direct queries, in settings or metrics E's verdicts did not count

record.tranche_reason: The study tests concept unlearning under different prompt types and evaluates whether selecting the worst prompt type improves performance across prompts. It does not test the specified fine-tuning, activation-ablation, or quantization recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports concept-accuracy results after its own unlearning methods and under different prompt types, including unseen prompt types. Its prompt-type accuracy selection is part of training, not a separate recovery attack; the reported post-training prompt-type results are included. Comparisons and cited results not produced by the study are not recorded.
record.test_reason: A new concept-unlearning method (MPTune/MPSelectTune). Only its SciQ-WMDP-Bio results bear on a version: version A, whether bio-weapons QA accuracy falls to near chance while general ability is kept. The robustness checks vary only in-context exemplar prompt types. There are no fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, jailbreak or language attacks. Gender and race 'concept' prediction from input text (BIOS, RT-Gender, ToxicBias, Adult) is a classification ability on the input, not hidden stored knowledge, so those results fit no version. The study's link to the claim is weak and indirect.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that two-stage fine-tuning, with a second stage on the prompt type with the highest concept accuracy, lowers average and worst-case concept accuracy toward chance. Worst-case concept accuracy falls by up to 17 points vs baselines while task accuracy and MMLU are kept. The method outperforms ICUL, SKU and ECK baselines. The generalization-to-unseen-prompt-types claim rests on one setting (LLaMA-2, BIOS).
record.recipe_differences: Uses PEFT fine-tuning with a joint task-and-concept objective, then fine-tunes on the worst-performing prompt type; it does not reproduce the cited unlearning recipes or the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt type and exemplar count/selection affect concept accuracy. The study also reports results for prompt types held out from training.

fits_no_version.finding: After multi-prompt unlearning (MPTune), BIOS gender prediction stays at up to 72.1% on some prompt types while others sit near 50% chance. Authors read this as the model not having truly unlearned. Worst-prompt fine-tuning lowers the peak to 62.7%. On held-out prompt types, averages are 58.0%/56.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning of input-derived sensitive attributes (e.g., gender) is prompt-dependent: residual attribute prediction resurfaces under specific in-context exemplar configurations.

record.problems: The claim-relevant robustness evidence is limited to prompt-type changes. No error bars or other uncertainty estimates are reported. Some prompt-specific results are shown in figures; the text gives selected extrema and averages rather than every prompt-specific value.
record.rows_left_out: The full Table 1 and appendix prompt-specific figure results include many additional method, dataset, model, and metric combinations; they were not extracted because the flattened table layout does not reliably support assigning every value to its model and metric. The record retains the explicitly described prompt-type results and the clearly laid-out SciQ-WMDP-Bio Table 6 results.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover WMDP-Bio knowledge: no relearning, ablation, quantization, jailbreak or language tests. Only exemplar prompt-type variation (Fig. 6), whose model mapping is unclear.
Entirely untested: no post-unlearning fine-tuning recovery.
Entirely untested: no activation ablation or access-vs-deletion analysis.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context disclosure attacks on bio-weapons knowledge. Prompt-type variation on WMDP is only in Fig. 6 and was not extracted.
The method is not tested against the fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or jailbreak attacks above. Robustness is shown only across exemplar prompt types, mostly on gender tasks.

missing.what: MMLU accuracy after unlearning on SciQ-WMDP-Bio. Llama-2: 43.9 to 24.0/24.3; Llama-3.1: 65.0 to 64.1/64.3; Mistral: 56.1 to 51.7/52.1. Needed for A's general-ability part.
Prompt-type-specific concept accuracies on SciQ-WMDP-Bio for Aug, MPTune and MPSelectTune. Residual bio-weapons accuracy reaches about 40% vs 25% chance on some prompt types; model unstated.
Held-out prompt-type per-prompt concept accuracies (BIOS, LLaMA-2), not only averages.

record.verdict_notes: Reader used V1/V5/V6 codes; these are remapped. Most of the paper concerns gender and race concept removal from input text, which is not the hidden-knowledge construct of the versions. Only the SciQ-WMDP-Bio results bear on A, and the paper never attacks the unlearned bio knowledge with B–E methods. The F claim (robust counter-method) is not established by these tests. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Some Figure 6 values appear to come from small samples (multiples of about 4.5%).

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the named unlearning methods in the claim (gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU). It tests its own concept-unlearning method and baselines; the attack-resistance component is limited to prompt-type variation.
No post-unlearning recovery fine-tuning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis establishing access-blocking rather than deletion.
Tests prompt-type variation in exemplar count and selection, including unseen prompt types. Does not test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context disclosure of the forgotten information.
Tests the proposed method against prompt-type variation and unseen prompt types only; does not test resistance to fine-tuning recovery, activation edits, quantization, jailbreaks, or other languages.

tranche.reason: A new concept-unlearning method with SciQ-WMDP-Bio results on version A in a new joint-prompt setting. The reader's T2 is also arguable, but T3 is acceptable.

source_check.notes: Table 6 (Appendix A.4) is the only evidence for version A. Its concept task is WMDP-Bio MCQ answered jointly with SciQ in a few-shot prompt, not standard WMDP evaluation. The text says MMLU 'remains stable for all models', but Llama-2 falls 43.9 -> 24.0/24.3 and Mistral by about 4 points. Per-prompt SciQ-WMDP-Bio results (Figure 6) are figure-only. No recovery attacks.

statements.correction: 2607.03932 (preprint, no code): Llama-3.1-8B, SciQ-WMDP-Bio joint-prompt 4-choice MCQ (chance 25%). Concept (bio-weapons) accuracy 61.3 -> 31.8 (MPTune) and 29.9 (MPSelectTune). SciQ task accuracy 68.4 -> 75.6/75.4. MMLU 65.0 -> 64.1/64.3. LoRA fine-tuning, no recovery attack.
statements.problem: The statement cites r8 and r9 from this study but never names or describes it. It gives no numbers for it, and its 'why' counts only four studies (OBLIVIATE, ELM, PINT, TRACE). Readers cannot see what this study adds.

LLaMA-2-7B, BIOS gender (chance 50%). MPTune: worst type '2, half_random' 72.1%, best '5, sim_dissim' 49.6%, all-type average 61.57%, SD 5.51. MPSelectTune: peak 62.7%, SD 4.35, average 55.6%.
